## <mark>Prognostic Factors in Melanoma</mark>

### Microstaging (See Table 124-4)

<mark>**TUMOR THICKNESS**</mark>  
<mark>The single most important prognostic factor for survival and clinical management in localized stage I and II cutaneous melanoma is **tumor thickness**.[68] As originally described by Breslow, tumor thickness is measured from the top of the granular layer of the epidermis to the greatest depth of tumor invasion, using an ocular micrometer and reported in millimeters (see eFig.</mark> <mark>124-17.1 in online edition).</mark> <mark>Survival decreases with increasing Breslow depth.</mark>

**Clark level** is an alternate, less accurate method of assessing tumor invasion based on anatomic level and is no longer the primary criterion in modern staging. Historically described by Clark, the levels are:
- **Level I**: Melanoma confined to the epidermis (in situ)
- **Level II**: Extension into the papillary dermis
- **Level III**: Tumor fills and expands the papillary dermis
- **Level IV**: Invasion into the reticular dermis
- **Level V**: Invasion into the subcutaneous fat

While Clark level may influence prognosis in thin melanomas (<1 mm), where levels IV or V can upstage a tumor from T1a to T1b, evidence suggests it is a weaker prognostic indicator compared to Breslow thickness.[69]

**ULCERATION**  
Ulceration is currently recognized as an independent prognostic factor in primary melanoma. Its presence worsens prognosis and is incorporated into the AJCC staging system. Ulceration is defined histologically as disruption of the epidermis overlying the melanoma, associated with tumor-induced necrosis rather than trauma. It carries significant weight in microstaging and upstaging of melanomas, particularly in tumors of intermediate thickness.

## <mark>Prognostic Factors in Distant Metastasis</mark>

<mark>The presence of distant metastases portends the worst prognosis, with mean survival rates measured in months rather than years.</mark> Site of metastasis is the most important prognostic factor in the AJCC melanoma staging system; visceral metastases are associated with a poorer prognosis compared to non-visceral sites (such as skin, subcutaneous tissue, and distant lymph nodes). <mark>Other significant prognostic variables include the number of metastatic sites and surgical resectability.</mark> Solitary metastases that are resected after radiologic confirmation of stability over 3 to 6 months have been associated with prolonged survival in some patients, although there is no strong evidence to date that asymptomatic detection improves overall survival. <mark>Elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels are also associated with a worse prognosis.</mark>

## Clinical Course

### Stages I and II Melanoma

The prognosis for patients with thin primary melanoma (< 1 mm in Breslow depth) and localized disease is excellent, with long-term survival achieved in more than 90% of cases. However, approximately 15% to 36% of patients with stage I or II melanoma will experience local, regional, or distant recurrence during their clinical course. Melanoma typically recurs in a predictable pattern—first locally and regionally, then at distant sites. Notably, melanoma can also bypass regional lymph nodes through direct hematogenous dissemination.

<mark>Most recurrences occur within the first 1 to 5 years after diagnosis and treatment, depending on tumor thickness and other prognostic features of the primary lesion.</mark> Nonetheless, late recurrences (10 or more years after initial diagnosis) occur in approximately 1% to 5% of cases. The majority of tumors associated with late recurrence are of intermediate thickness (mean 1.6 mm, typically ranging from 0.70 to 3.0 mm), with a mean time to recurrence of 14.3 years. "Ultra-late" recurrences occurring more than 15 years after diagnosis are extremely rare but have been documented.

### Stage III Melanoma

Data from the Sunbelt Melanoma Trial involving over 1,100 patients show that recurrence rates are significantly higher in early stage III melanoma (micrometastatic nodal disease detected by sentinel lymph node biopsy) compared to SLN-negative melanoma (15.5% vs. 6.0%, respectively). Patients with SLN-positive disease are also more likely to develop distant metastases rather than locoregional recurrence alone (67% vs. 46%). Pooled analyses estimate 5-year overall survival rates of 93% to 88% for SLN-negative patients, compared to 51% to 67% for those with a positive SLN.

Stage III melanoma represents a heterogeneous group of patients with highly variable clinical outcomes. This diversity is reflected in 5-year survival rates, which range from 70% for patients with microscopic nodal involvement to significantly lower rates in those with more extensive nodal or in-transit disease.

# <mark>Prognostic Factors in Melanoma</mark>

## Age
Males over 60 years of age have the highest mortality rates from melanoma. Older patients tend to present with thicker primary tumors and a higher proportion of ulcerated melanomas. Even after adjusting for these factors, age remains an independent prognostic factor. It has been suggested that age may act as a surrogate for declining host immune defense mechanisms.

## Gender
Numerous studies have shown that women have better survival rates than men, even after controlling for tumor thickness and anatomic site.

## Anatomic Site
The location of the primary cutaneous melanoma has been variably associated with survival outcomes. In the AJCC study, melanomas on the trunk, head, and neck were linked to a worse prognosis compared to those on the extremities, although the classification grouped sites broadly into (1) extremities or (2) trunk, head, or neck. Another large study of 5093 patients found that melanomas on the back, thorax, upper neck, and scalp (BANS regions) were associated with significantly lower survival rates compared to those on the lower trunk, thigh, lower leg, feet, lower arms, hands, and face. However, anatomic site has not consistently been confirmed as an independent prognostic factor across studies.

# Prognostic Factors in Regional Metastasis

<mark>The status of the regional lymph nodes is the most powerful prognostic factor for survival in melanoma.</mark> <mark>The presence of regional lymph node metastasis is associated with a poorer prognosis.</mark> <mark>The number of involved lymph nodes, regardless of size, is the most significant risk factor.</mark>

# <mark>Thrombocytopenia in Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS)</mark>

<mark>The thrombocytopenia in Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS) is persistent, with platelet counts typically ranging from 1,000 to 80,000 platelets per μL.</mark> <mark>A platelet count of <70,000/μL is required to meet formal diagnostic criteria.</mark> The platelets are characteristically small in size, and platelet aggregation is defective. 

<mark>Immunoglobulin levels are abnormal: IgM and sometimes IgG are low, and isohemagglutinins are absent.</mark> <mark>In contrast, IgA, IgE, and IgD levels are usually elevated.</mark> <mark>Hematologic abnormalities such as eosinophilia, leukopenia, and lymphopenia are commonly observed.</mark> <mark>Delayed hypersensitivity skin-test reactivity is diminished, and patients fail to respond to polysaccharide antigens.</mark>

## Prognosis, Clinical Course, and Treatment

With modern therapeutic interventions, some patients with WAS survive into adulthood; however, a significant proportion die before age 10 due to hemorrhage, infection, malignancy, or complications of transplantation. Approximately 13% of patients develop lymphoreticular malignancies, particularly non-Hodgkin lymphoma, often with extranodal and central nervous system involvement. The development of autoimmune hemolytic anemia is a poor prognostic indicator and is associated with an increased risk of lymphoid malignancies; overall, 25% of patients with autoimmunity go on to develop malignancy. About 10% of patients die from these malignancies, typically during adolescence or early adulthood.

Female carriers of WAS mutations can be identified by selective inactivation of the abnormal X chromosome in T cells, B cells, and platelets. Analysis of maternal X-chromosome inactivation patterns has also been used to diagnose atypical cases in males. Mutation analysis enables prenatal diagnosis.

Management includes appropriate use of antibiotics, immunizations, and transfusions of platelets and plasma to reduce the risk of fatal infections and hemorrhage. Intravenous γ-globulin infusions are beneficial in some patients. Splenectomy may be considered for severe, recurrent bleeding, but it increases the risk of infection from encapsulated bacteria, especially in patients unable to respond to vaccines. 

Bone marrow or stem cell transplantation is the treatment of choice for patients with recurrent complications, particularly significant autoimmunity. Successful engraftment leads to normalization of platelet count and function, restoration of immune function, and resolution of dermatitis (dependent on T lymphocyte engraftment). The 5-year survival rate with HLA-matched sibling donors is 87%.

Topical glucocorticoids and systemic γ-globulin may improve dermatitis. Chronic oral acyclovir is recommended for patients with recurrent eczema herpeticum.

# Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)

## At a Glance

- Heterogeneous group of X-linked and autosomal recessive disorders characterized by defective cell-mediated and humoral immunity.  
- Clinical features: failure to thrive in infancy, chronic diarrhea, recurrent mucocutaneous candidiasis, and severe bacterial and viral infections.  
- High risk of graft-versus-host disease.  
- Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can prevent early death.

## Epidemiology

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) comprises a group of heterogeneous disorders with similar clinical and immunologic features—profound deficiencies in both humoral and cell-mediated immunity. The overall incidence is approximately 1 in 75,000 live births. Inheritance patterns include X-linked and autosomal recessive forms.

## Pathogenesis

All patients with SCID share core clinical features and exhibit defects in both T-cell and B-cell immunity, though the severity varies. The molecular basis of SCID involves disruptions in critical steps of T-cell development (see Table 144-4). A specific genetic defect is identified in about 95% of cases.

X-linked SCID accounts for approximately 46% of cases and results from mutations in the gene encoding the γc chain of the IL-2 receptor. This γc chain is a shared component of seven cytokine receptors (including those for IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21), explaining the profound impact on lymphocyte development and function.

Because these cytokine signals are essential for early T-cell development, female carriers exhibit skewed X-chromosome inactivation: T cells expressing the mutated allele fail to survive, leading to selective advantage of T cells with the normal allele.

# <mark>Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome</mark>

## <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

- <mark>**Inheritance**: X-linked recessive</mark>  
- **Gene**: Mutations in *WAS* (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome gene)  
- **Classic clinical triad**:  
  <mark>- Recalcitrant dermatitis</mark>  
  <mark>- Recurrent pyogenic infections</mark>  
  <mark>- Hemorrhage due to thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction</mark>  
- <mark>**Therapy**: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (bone marrow transplantation)</mark>

---

## Immunological Features

Patients with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) exhibit multiple immune cell defects, including:  
- <mark>Impaired **NK cell cytotoxicity**</mark>  
- Defective **dendritic cell migration and activation**  
- **Impaired macrophage chemotaxis**

These contribute to the broad susceptibility to infections and immune dysregulation seen in the disease.

---

## Clinical Findings

<mark>The classic triad of hemorrhage, recurrent pyogenic infections, and recalcitrant dermatitis is present in only **25% of patients**.</mark> However, individual manifestations are common:

### Bleeding Diathesis
- <mark>Present in **84% of patients**, making it the most frequent manifestation</mark>  
- <mark>Typically appears in the **first weeks or months of life**</mark>  
- Common presentations:  
  <mark>- Bloody diarrhea (often initial sign)</mark>  
  - Epistaxis  
  - Hematemesis  
  - Hematuria  
  - Mucocutaneous petechiae  
  - Intracranial hemorrhage  

Thrombocytopenia is **persistent**, with platelet counts ranging from **1,000 to 80,000/μL**.  
- **Diagnostic criterion**: Platelet count < **70,000/μL**  
- Platelets are characteristically **small (microthrombocytopenia)**  
- Platelet aggregation is defective

---

### Infections
- <mark>Recurrent **bacterial infections** begin in infancy as maternal antibodies wane</mark>  
- Common infections:  
  - Furunculosis  
  - Conjunctivitis  
  - Otitis media and externa  
  - Pansinusitis  
  - Pneumonia  
  - Meningitis  
  - Septicemia  

- Predominant pathogens: **Encapsulated bacteria**  
  - *Streptococcus pneumoniae*  
  - *Haemophilus influenzae*  
  - *Neisseria meningitidis*  

- Increased susceptibility to:  
  - Herpesviruses and other viruses  
  - *Pneumocystis jirovecii* (formerly *P. carinii*)

---

### Dermatitis
- <mark>Occurs in **~80% of patients**</mark>  
- Typically develops in the **first few months of life**  
- Often **severe and widespread**  
- Commonly affects:  
  - Face  
  - Scalp  
  - Flexural areas  

- Features distinguishing it from typical atopic dermatitis:  
  - More **exfoliative**  
  - **Serosanguineous crusting**  
  - Frequent **lichenification**  

- Complications:  
  - Secondary bacterial infection  
  - **Eczema herpeticum**  
  - **Molluscum contagiosum**  

- Additional IgE-mediated conditions:  
  - Urticaria  
  - Food allergies  
  - Asthma

---

### Autoimmune Manifestations
- Occur in **up to 40% of patients**  
- Most common:  
  - **Vasculitis** (20%) – affecting skin, GI tract, brain, heart  
  - **Autoimmune hemolytic anemia** (14%)  
  - **IgA nephropathy** (up to 10%)  

- Other immune-mediated conditions:  
  - Angioedema  
  - Dermatomyositis  
  - Pyoderma gangrenosum  
  - Erythema nodosum  

- Hepatosplenomegaly is common  
- Lymphadenopathy, transient arthritis, and joint effusions may occur

---

## Laboratory Findings

- **Thrombocytopenia** with **small platelets**  
- **Immunoglobulin abnormalities**:  
  - ↓ IgM (common)  
  - ↓ IgG (sometimes)  
  - Absent isohemagglutinins  
  - ↑ IgA, IgE, IgD  

- Impaired humoral and cellular immunity contributes to infection susceptibility and autoimmunity

--- 

*Note: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only curative therapy and is recommended early in the disease course.*

# <mark>CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS</mark>

## <mark>Presentation</mark>

<mark>The presence of any friable, non-healing lesion should raise the suspicion of skin cancer.</mark> Frequently, basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is diagnosed in patients who report that the lesion bled briefly, then healed completely, only to recur later. <mark>BCC typically develops on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck but can occur anywhere on the body.</mark> <mark>Common features include translucency, ulceration, telangiectasias, and a rolled border.</mark> Clinical characteristics vary among sub-types, which include nodular, superficial, morpheaform (sclerosing), pigmented BCC, and fibroepithelioma of Pinkus (FEP).

## Basal Cell Carcinoma Sub-Types

### Nodular Basal Cell Carcinoma

Nodular BCC is the most common clinical sub-type (Fig. 115-1). It typically occurs on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck and presents as a translucent papule or nodule, depending on duration. Telangiectasias are commonly present, and the lesion often has a rolled border. Larger lesions with central necrosis are historically referred to as rodent ulcers (Fig. 115-2). The differential diagnosis includes traumatized dermal nevus and amelanotic melanoma.

### Pigmented Basal Cell Carcinoma

Pigmented BCC is a variant of nodular BCC characterized by increased melanization. It appears as a hyperpigmented, translucent papule and may be eroded (Fig. 115-3). The differential diagnosis primarily includes nodular melanoma.

### Superficial Basal Cell Carcinoma

Superficial BCC most commonly occurs on the trunk and presents as an erythematous, well-demarcated patch that may resemble eczema (Fig. 115-4). An isolated patch of "eczema" that fails to respond to topical treatment should prompt suspicion for superficial BCC.

### Morpheaform (Sclerosing) Basal Cell Carcinoma

Morpheaform BCC is an aggressive variant with distinct clinical and histologic features. Lesions often have an ivory-white appearance and may resemble a scar or a small, indurated plaque (Fig. 115-5). This sub-type is more infiltrative and has a higher risk of recurrence.

## Perineural Spread

<mark>A higher incidence of perineural spread has been reported in some studies, with Leibovitch et al.</mark> <mark>noting involvement in more than 50 percent of periocular basal cell carcinomas (BCCs), often leading to orbital invasion.</mark> <mark>These aggressive tumors frequently require extensive surgical intervention, including orbital exenteration in severe cases.</mark> Perineural spread may present clinically with pain, paresthesias, muscle weakness, or paralysis. The presence of focal neurologic symptoms at the site of a previously treated skin cancer should raise suspicion for nerve involvement.

## <mark>Metastasis</mark>

<mark>Metastasis of BCC is rare, occurring in only 0.0028 to 0.55 percent of cases.</mark> <mark>Lymph node and lung involvement are the most common sites of metastatic spread.</mark> <mark>In a series by Von Domarus et al., three out of five patients with metastatic BCC had histologic evidence of perineural or intravascular invasion.</mark> <mark>Squamous differentiation was not seen in the primary tumors but was present in two of the five metastatic cases.</mark> <mark>Overall, squamous differentiation was observed in 15 percent of primary or metastatic tumors among 170 reviewed cases.</mark> <mark>Aggressive histologic features—such as morpheaform growth pattern, squamous metaplasia, and perineural invasion—are recognized risk factors for metastasis.</mark>

## Diagnosis

Diagnosis of BCC is based on accurate histopathologic interpretation of skin biopsy specimens. Shave biopsy is often sufficient and preferred; a sterilized razor blade allows precise control over biopsy depth and is frequently superior to a No. 15 scalpel for this technique. Punch biopsy is particularly useful for evaluating flat lesions, such as morpheaform BCC, or recurrent tumors arising within a scar.

## Histopathology

Histopathologic features vary by subtype, but most BCCs share common characteristics. The malignant basaloid cells typically have large nuclei with scant cytoplasm. Despite nuclear enlargement, overt nuclear atypia may be minimal, and mitotic figures are usually rare or absent. A hallmark feature is stromal retraction around tumor nests, creating peritumoral lacunae, which aids in diagnosis.

### Nodular Basal Cell Carcinoma

Nodular BCC is the most common subtype, accounting for approximately 50 percent of cases. It is characterized by well-circumscribed nodules of basophilic tumor cells and prominent stromal retraction (Fig. 115-8A). Micronodular BCC refers to tumors composed of multiple small nodules less than 15 μm in diameter (Fig. 115-8B), which may have a higher risk of recurrence due to less distinct margins.

### Pigmented Basal Cell Carcinoma

Pigmented BCC shares histologic features with nodular BCC but includes melanin deposition. Melanocytes are found interspersed among tumor cells and contain abundant melanin granules in their cytoplasm and dendrites. While tumor cells themselves contain little melanin, the surrounding stroma often harbors numerous melanophages. Although about 75 percent of BCCs contain melanocytes, significant pigmentation is present in only about 25 percent of cases.

### Superficial Basal Cell Carcinoma

Superficial BCC is characterized by small buds of malignant basaloid cells extending from the epidermal basal layer into the upper dermis. The peripheral cells typically show palisading, and epidermal atrophy may be present. Dermal invasion is usually minimal. This subtype is most commonly found on the trunk and extremities but can also occur on the head and neck.

# GUIDELINES ## 2019 IUSTI-Europe guideline for the management of anogenital warts ### Abstract This guideline is an update of the 2011 European Guideline for the Management of Anogenital Warts. It aims to support best practice in the care of patients with anogenital warts by providing evidence-based recommendations on diagnosis, treatment, follow-up, and patient advice. It is intended for use by healthcare professionals in sexual health or dermato-venereology clinics in Europe, though it may be adapted for other settings where anogenital warts are managed. As a European guideline, recommendations should be adapted according to national circumstances and healthcare systems. Despite the availability of vaccines preventing HPV types 6 and 11—responsible for >95% of anogenital warts—these lesions remain a common and significant health issue. A previous systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on anogenital wart treatments was updated. Key updates in this guideline include: - Updated background on the prevalence, natural history, and transmission of HPV infection and anogenital warts - Grading of key recommendations based on the strength of recommendation and quality of evidence - Evaluation and inclusion of 5-fluorouracil, local interferon, and photodynamic therapy as potential second-line treatment options - Updated evidence on the impact of HPV vaccination on anogenital wart incidence ### Introduction and methodology This document updates the 2011 European Guideline for the Management of Anogenital Warts. It provides evidence-based guidance on diagnosis, treatment, follow-up, and patient counseling to support optimal clinical care. The target audience includes healthcare professionals working in sexual health or dermatology clinics across Europe, although the guideline may be adapted for use in other settings. Recommendations should be tailored to national contexts and healthcare systems. Clinicians and service providers are encouraged to develop local treatment algorithms that reflect their specific resources, treatment availability, and patient population needs. The treatment recommendations from the 2011 guideline were based on a systematic review of RCTs. They are caused primarily by infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly low-risk types 6 and 11, which account for over 95% of cases. HPV is transmitted through direct skin-to-skin or mucosal contact, typically during sexual activity. Transmission can occur even in the absence of visible warts, due to subclinical or latent infection. The incubation period varies widely, ranging from weeks to months, and spontaneous regression may occur. Factors associated with increased risk include young age, multiple sexual partners, and immunosuppression (e.g., HIV infection).

# 2012 European guideline for the management of anogenital warts

## Abstract

<mark>**Background**</mark>  
<mark>Although new HPV vaccines have been developed and are in the process of implementation, anogenital warts remain a very frequent problem in clinical practice.</mark>

**Objective**  
To update previously published European guidelines for the management of anogenital warts.

**Methods**  
A systematic review of randomized controlled trials for anogenital warts was conducted. The primary data were analyzed and collated, and the findings were formulated into a clinical guideline. The draft was reviewed by the IUSTI Europe Editorial Board and made available online for public comment; feedback was incorporated into the final version.

<mark>**Results**</mark>  
<mark>The data confirm that only surgical therapies achieve primary clearance rates approaching 100%.</mark> <mark>Recurrences—包括 previously treated sites or new lesions—occur after all treatments, with recurrence rates often 20–30% or higher.</mark> All treatment modalities are associated with local skin reactions such as itching, burning, erosions, and pain.

<mark>**Conclusions**</mark>  
Physicians managing patients with genital warts should develop individualized treatment algorithms based on local practices and guidelines. Patient management should include clinical review at least every 4 weeks, with a change in therapy if there is an inadequate response. Patients with first-episode warts should be offered screening for other sexually transmitted infections. Management must also include partner notification and health promotion.

---

## <mark>Aetiology and transmission</mark>

<mark>Anogenital warts (also known as genital warts, condylomata acuminata, or condylomas) are benign proliferative lesions caused primarily by human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11, which are detected in >90% of cases.</mark> <mark>Co-infection with high-risk HPV types, such as HPV 16, is common.</mark> <mark>Genital warts are transmitted sexually, with an estimated transmission rate of approximately 60% between untreated sexual partners.</mark>

This guideline was developed on behalf of:
- The European Branch of the International Union against Sexually Transmitted Infections (IUSTI Europe)
- The European Dermatology Federation (EDF)
- The Union of European Medical Specialists (UEMS)

---

## <mark>Clinical features</mark>

### <mark>Symptoms</mark>

<mark>Most patients are asymptomatic aside from the visible presence of lesions.</mark> <mark>When symptoms occur, they may include itching, bleeding, fissuring, or dyspareunia.</mark>

### <mark>Physical signs</mark>

<mark>Lesions typically appear at sites subject to trauma during intercourse.</mark> <mark>They may be solitary, but multiple lesions (usually 5–15) measuring 1–5 mm in diameter are more common.</mark> <mark>Warts can coalesce into larger plaques, particularly in immunosuppressed individuals or those with diabetes.</mark>

<mark>In uncircumcised men, the preputial cavity—including the glans penis, coronal sulcus, frenulum, and inner foreskin—is most frequently affected.</mark> <mark>In circumcised men, the penile shaft is more commonly involved.</mark> <mark>Other sites include the urethral meatus, pubis, scrotum, groin, perineum, perianal area, and anal canal.</mark>

<mark>In women, warts may occur on the fourchette, labia minora, labia majora, pubis, clitoris, urethral meatus, perineum, perianal region, anal canal, introitus, vagina, and ectocervix.</mark>

<mark>Intra-anal warts are most frequently seen in individuals who practice receptive anal intercourse, though they can occur without it.</mark> <mark>Warts are rarely found proximal to the dentate line.</mark>

<mark>Anogenital warts vary in color from pink or salmon red to white, greyish-white, or various shades of brown (pigmented lesions).</mark> <mark>Pigmentation is more commonly observed on the labia majora, penile shaft, pubis, groin, perineum, and perianal area.</mark>

---

## Complications

### Physical and psychosexual implications

Anogenital warts are often perceived as disfiguring and can significantly affect sexual well-being. Patients may experience anxiety, guilt, anger, and reduced self-esteem. Common concerns include potential effects on fertility and cancer risk.

### Pre-cancer and cancer

Premalignant conditions—such as vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN), anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN), and penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN)—as well as invasive cancers (vulval, anal, and penile) may coexist with anogenital warts, develop within them, or be initially misdiagnosed as warts. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for such conditions, especially in persistent, atypical, or treatment-resistant lesions.

## <mark>Scissors Excision and Other Treatment Modalities</mark>

<mark>Scissors excision is useful when smaller numbers of lesions are present and may be assisted by diathermy to control bleeding and to destroy any residual wart tissue.</mark> <mark>Clearance rates of 94–100% for electrosurgery and 89–100% for scissors excision have been reported, with recurrence rates ranging from 19–29%.</mark>

Curettage is a simple and effective technique for treating a small number of lesions, with either diathermy or silver nitrate used for hemostasis. <mark>Carbon dioxide and YAG lasers deliver very high power densities to small tissue volumes.</mark> <mark>Both electrosurgery and laser surgery should be performed using surgical masks by the treatment team and with the aid of a smoke evacuator.</mark> No suitable randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating curettage or laser therapy were identified.

### Formal Surgery (IVc)

Bulky warts, extensive warts, anal or intra-anal warts, and significant lesions in children are best managed under general anesthesia by an appropriate surgical specialist.

## Therapies Not Generally Recommended

The routine use of **podophyllin** or **interferons** is not recommended. Podophyllin (20–25%), a non-standardized resin extract from the *Podophyllum* plant, is inexpensive but has only moderate efficacy. Up to 10% of podophyllin contains mutagenic compounds such as quercetin and kaempferol. Severe systemic toxicity following topical application has been reported, including fatalities, intrauterine death, teratogenicity, and neurological complications.

In specialist settings, **α-** and **β-interferons** may be used as adjuvants to surgery in difficult cases. A recent systematic review supports the use of topical or intralesional interferon. Combination therapies are commonly used in clinical practice, and further evaluation of these approaches is warranted.

## Treatment Algorithms

Clinicians managing patients with genital warts should have access to both patient-applied (home) and provider-administered (clinic-based) therapies. The choice of treatment should be based on the morphology and extent of warts and made collaboratively between the clinician and patient.

Patients with limited disease (1–5 warts) often prefer immediate in-clinic treatment. Since genital warts may regress spontaneously, watchful waiting is a valid option at any anatomical site. A simple treatment algorithm is provided below.

### Management of Specific Wart Locations

- **Vaginal warts**: Can be treated with trichloroacetic acid (TCA) or cryotherapy.  
- **Cervical warts**: Should be managed by a gynecologist.  
- **Intra-meatal warts**: Treatable with TCA or various surgical techniques.  
- **Intra-anal warts**: Small-volume lesions may be treated with TCA. Imiquimod is feasible with motivated patients. Otherwise, formal surgical referral is indicated.

## Treatment in Pregnancy

Genital warts may enlarge and multiply during pregnancy. The presence of warts at delivery carries an approximate risk of 1 in 400 for the infant developing juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis. There is no evidence that treating maternal warts reduces this risk, although reducing viral load may be prudent. Coordination with the obstetrician is recommended. Spontaneous regression of genital warts is commonly observed in the postpartum period.

## Treatment in Immunocompromised Patients

Both **HIV infection** and **iatrogenic immunosuppression** are associated with higher prevalence of anogenital warts. Treatment response is often suboptimal in HIV-positive individuals, and recurrence rates are increased.

Recent studies show total clearance rates of 31–32% with imiquimod in patients on HAART. One RCT reported 100% primary clearance with a combination of surgery and imiquimod.

## Partner Notification

- Current sexual partners, and if possible, partners from the past 6 months, should be evaluated for visible lesions.  
- Partners should also receive education and counseling regarding sexually transmitted diseases and prevention strategies.

## <mark>Sweet Syndrome</mark>

<mark>A constellation of symptoms and findings: the acute onset of fever, neutrophilia, erythematous, and tender skin lesions that typically show an upper dermal infiltrate of mature neutrophils.</mark>  
Cardiovascular, central nervous system, gastrointestinal, hepatic, musculoskeletal, ocular, oral, otic, pulmonary, renal, and splenic organs can be involved.  

### Clinical Subtypes
- **Classic (idiopathic) Sweet syndrome**: May be associated with infection of the upper respiratory and/or gastrointestinal tract, inflammatory bowel disease, and pregnancy.  
- **Malignancy-associated Sweet syndrome**: Occurs in individuals with previously undiagnosed or relapsing hematologic malignancies (e.g., acute myeloid leukemia) and solid tumors; presents as a cutaneous paraneoplastic syndrome.  
- **Drug-induced Sweet syndrome**: Develops after initiation of certain medications—most commonly granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF), but also all-trans retinoic acid, antibiotics, and others.  

### Pathogenesis
Cytokines (e.g., granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, interleukin-3, tumor necrosis factor-alpha) may play a key role in the recruitment and activation of neutrophils, contributing to the inflammatory cascade seen in the skin and systemic manifestations.

### Clinical Features
#### Cutaneous Lesions
<mark>Skin lesions typically appear as tender, red, or purple-red papules, nodules, or plaques.</mark> <mark>The eruption may present as a single lesion or multiple lesions, often distributed asymmetrically.</mark> <mark>Lesions may coalesce into larger plaques and can be accompanied by vesicles, pustules, or bullae.</mark>  

Extracutaneous involvement may affect:
- Musculoskeletal (arthralgia, myalgia)
- Ocular (conjunctivitis, uveitis)
- Oral (ulcers)
- Gastrointestinal, pulmonary, renal, and other organ systems

### <mark>Diagnosis</mark>
<mark>Based on clinical, laboratory, and histopathological findings.</mark> <mark>Major criteria include:</mark>
- <mark>Abrupt onset of painful erythematous plaques or nodules</mark>
- <mark>Histopathology showing a dense dermal infiltrate of mature neutrophils without vasculitis</mark>

<mark>Minor criteria:</mark>
- <mark>Preceding infection, pregnancy, malignancy, or drug exposure</mark>
- <mark>Fever (>38°C)</mark>
- <mark>Response to systemic corticosteroids</mark>
- <mark>Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, or neutrophilia</mark>

### Treatment
#### First-line systemic agents:
- **Corticosteroids** (e.g., prednisone 0.5–1.5 mg/kg/day): Rapid and effective response
- **Colchicine**: Alternative for mild cases or steroid-sparing
- **Potassium iodide**: Effective for some patients with localized or refractory disease

#### Local therapy:
- **Topical high-potency corticosteroids**
- **Intralesional corticosteroid injections**: Useful for localized or persistent lesions

Relapse may occur with tapering of therapy, particularly in malignancy-associated cases. Underlying conditions (e.g., infection, malignancy) should be investigated and managed appropriately.

## <mark>Histopathology of Sweet Syndrome</mark>

<mark>Although the dermal inflammation is usually dense and diffuse, it can also be perivascular or show "secondary" changes of leukocytoclastic vasculitis, which are considered epiphenomena and not indicative of a primary vasculitis.</mark> <mark>Neutrophilic spongiotic vesicles or subcorneal pustules result from exocytosis of neutrophils into the epidermis.</mark> <mark>When neutrophils are located entirely or partially within the subcutaneous fat, the condition is termed subcutaneous Sweet syndrome.</mark>

## Other Laboratory Tests

Peripheral leukocytosis with neutrophilia and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate are the most consistent laboratory findings in Sweet syndrome. However, leukocytosis may be absent in some patients with biopsy-confirmed disease. In cases of malignancy-associated Sweet syndrome, findings such as anemia, neutropenia, or abnormal platelet counts may occur.

A complete blood cell count with leukocyte differential and platelet count, assessment of acute phase reactants (such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein), serum chemistries (to evaluate liver and kidney function), and urinalysis should be performed. Thyroid function testing is also recommended due to a well-documented association between thyroid disease and Sweet syndrome.

## Special Tests

### Evaluation for Extracutaneous Manifestations

Extracutaneous involvement in Sweet syndrome may lead to additional laboratory or imaging abnormalities. Patients with central nervous system involvement may show abnormalities on brain single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), computed tomography (CT), electroencephalography (EEG), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or cerebrospinal fluid analysis.

Those with renal or hepatic involvement may exhibit hematuria, proteinuria, or elevated hepatic enzymes. Pulmonary involvement may present with pleural effusions and culture-negative, corticosteroid-responsive pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiography.

### Malignancy Workup

Given the association between Sweet syndrome and underlying malignancy—particularly hematologic and solid tumors—a thorough malignancy evaluation should be considered, especially in atypical, recurrent, or refractory cases.

## Differential Diagnosis

### Clinical Differential Diagnosis (Box 31-1)

The skin and mucosal lesions of Sweet syndrome can resemble those of other conditions, necessitating careful clinical and histopathologic differentiation.

# <mark>Neutrophilic Dermatosis Variants and Clinical Features</mark>

## <mark>Pustular Eruption and Localized Forms</mark>

<mark>Some patients previously described as having the "pustular eruption of ulcerative colitis" may be more accurately classified within a clinical variant of **Sweet syndrome**.</mark>

<mark>**Neutrophilic dermatosis of the dorsal hands**, also known as **pustular vasculitis of the dorsal hands**, is a localized pustular variant of Sweet syndrome characterized by lesions predominantly confined to the dorsal aspects of the hands.</mark> <mark>The lesions are morphologically similar to those seen in classic Sweet syndrome and typically resolve rapidly with systemic corticosteroids and/or dapsone therapy.</mark> <mark>Many individuals with this variant also have concurrent lesions on the oral mucosa, arms, legs, back, or face.</mark>

## <mark>Subcutaneous Sweet Syndrome</mark>

<mark>The cutaneous manifestations of **subcutaneous Sweet syndrome** usually present as erythematous, tender dermal nodules on the extremities.</mark> <mark>When located on the legs, these nodules often mimic **erythema nodosum** (see Chap.</mark> 69). <mark>Given that Sweet syndrome can occur concurrently or sequentially with erythema nodosum, biopsy of new dermal nodules may be required to confirm the diagnosis—even in patients with a prior biopsy-confirmed history of Sweet syndrome.</mark> <mark>Diagnostic criteria are summarized in Table 31-2.</mark>

<mark>![Figure 31-3: Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis.</mark> <mark>Typical lesion consisting of coalescing, plaque-forming papules.</mark> A. <mark>Bright-red lesions on the neck.</mark> B. <mark>Lesion on the dorsum of the right hand exhibiting the "relief of a mountain range" feature.]</mark>

# Related Physical Findings

## Extracutaneous Manifestations (Table 31-3)

Sweet syndrome can involve multiple organ systems beyond the skin, including the:

- <mark>Bones (sterile osteomyelitis, particularly in children)</mark>
- <mark>Central nervous system</mark>
- Ears
- Eyes
- Kidneys
- <mark>Intestines</mark>
- Liver
- Heart
- Lungs
- Mouth
- Muscles
- Spleen

Ocular manifestations—such as conjunctivitis—may be the initial presentation of Sweet syndrome. However, ocular involvement is variable in classic cases and uncommon in malignancy-associated or drug-induced forms.

In contrast, **oral mucosal involvement** (e.g., painful ulcers) is more frequently observed in patients with **hematologic disorders** and is rare in classic Sweet syndrome. Oral lesions, like other extracutaneous manifestations, typically resolve with systemic corticosteroid therapy.

# <mark>ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS</mark>

<mark>The pathogenesis of Sweet syndrome may be multifactorial and remains to be definitively determined.</mark> <mark>A septic process is suggested by the accompanying fever and peripheral leukocytosis.</mark> Indeed, a bacterial infection may have a causative role because most patients with classic Sweet syndrome have a febrile upper respiratory tract infection or tonsillitis that precedes their skin lesions by 1 to 3 weeks. <mark>Also, Sweet syndrome patients with culture-confirmed and serology-confirmed *Yersinia enterocolitica* intestinal infection improve with systemic antibiotics.</mark>

<mark>Sweet syndrome may result from a hypersensitivity reaction to an eliciting bacterial, viral, or tumor antigen.</mark> The appearance, histopathology, and course of the skin lesions support this concept. <mark>In addition, the prompt response of both the symptoms and the lesions to corticosteroids further supports this hypothesis.</mark>

<mark>Leukotactic mechanisms, dermal dendrocytes, circulating autoantibodies, immune complexes, HLA serotypes, and cytokines have all been postulated to contribute to the pathogenesis of Sweet syndrome.</mark> Complement does not appear to be essential to the disease process. In some patients, antibodies to neutrophilic cytoplasmic antigens have been demonstrated; however, these are likely to represent an epiphenomenon.

On the other hand, cytokines—directly and/or indirectly—may have an etiologic role in the development of Sweet syndrome symptoms and lesions.

G-CSF, granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor, interferon-γ, interleukin-1, interleukin-3, interleukin-6, and interleukin-8 are potential cytokine candidates in the pathogenesis.

# <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS</mark>

## <mark>History</mark>

<mark>Sweet syndrome patients may appear dramatically ill.</mark> <mark>The skin eruption is usually accompanied by fever and leukocytosis.</mark> <mark>However, the skin disease can follow the fever by several days to weeks or be concurrently present with the fever throughout the episode of the dermatosis.</mark> Arthralgia, general malaise, headache, and myalgia are other associated symptoms.

## <mark>Acute Febrile Neutrophilic Dermatosis (Sweet Syndrome)</mark>

### <mark>At a Glance</mark>

<mark>A constellation of symptoms and findings: the acute onset of fever, neutrophilia, erythematous, and tender skin lesions that typically show an upper dermal infiltrate of mature neutrophils.</mark>  
Cardiovascular, central nervous system, gastrointestinal, hepatic, musculoskeletal, ocular, oral, otic, pulmonary, renal, and splenic organs can be involved.  
Classic Sweet syndrome may be associated with infection of the upper respiratory and/or gastrointestinal tract, inflammatory bowel disease, and pregnancy.

However, classic Sweet syndrome also occurs in younger adults and children. The youngest reported patients were brothers who developed the dermatosis at 10 and 15 days of age.

Several investigators consider it appropriate to distinguish between the classic form and the malignancy-associated form of this disease because the onset or recurrence of many cases is temporally associated with the discovery or relapse of cancer. Malignancy-associated Sweet syndrome does not have a female predominance and is most often associated with acute myelogenous leukemia. In Sweet syndrome patients with dermatosis-related solid tumors, carcinomas of the genitourinary organs, breast, and gastrointestinal tract are the most frequently occurring cancers.

A drug-induced variant of the dermatosis has also been described. It has most frequently been observed in association with the administration of granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF). However, several other medications have also been implicated in eliciting drug-induced Sweet syndrome.

# <mark>Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome</mark>

## <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

- <mark>**Inheritance**: X-linked recessive</mark>  
- **Gene**: Mutations in *WAS* (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome gene)  
- **Classic clinical triad**:  
  <mark>- Recalcitrant dermatitis</mark>  
  <mark>- Recurrent pyogenic infections</mark>  
  <mark>- Hemorrhage due to thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction</mark>  
- **Therapy**: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (bone marrow transplantation)

---

## Immunological Features

Patients with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) exhibit multiple immune cell defects, including:  
- <mark>Impaired **NK cell cytotoxicity**</mark>  
- Defective **dendritic cell migration and activation**  
- **Impaired macrophage chemotaxis**

These contribute to the broad susceptibility to infections and immune dysregulation seen in the disease.

---

## Clinical Findings

<mark>The classic triad of hemorrhage, recurrent pyogenic infections, and recalcitrant dermatitis is present in only **25% of patients**.</mark> However, individual manifestations are common:

### <mark>Bleeding Diathesis</mark>
- <mark>Present in **84% of patients**, making it the most frequent manifestation</mark>  
- <mark>Typically appears in the **first weeks or months of life**</mark>  
- <mark>Common presentations:</mark>  
  <mark>- Bloody diarrhea (often initial sign)</mark>  
  <mark>- Epistaxis</mark>  
  <mark>- Hematemesis</mark>  
  <mark>- Hematuria</mark>  
  <mark>- Mucocutaneous petechiae</mark>  
  <mark>- Intracranial hemorrhage</mark>  

Thrombocytopenia is **persistent**, with platelet counts ranging from **1,000 to 80,000/μL**.  
- **Diagnostic criterion**: Platelet count < **70,000/μL**  
- <mark>Platelets are characteristically **small (microthrombocytopenia)**</mark>  
- Platelet aggregation is defective

---

### Infections
- <mark>Recurrent **bacterial infections** begin in infancy as maternal antibodies wane</mark>  
- Common infections:  
  <mark>- Furunculosis</mark>  
  - Conjunctivitis  
  <mark>- Otitis media and externa</mark>  
  - Pansinusitis  
  <mark>- Pneumonia</mark>  
  - Meningitis  
  - Septicemia  

- Predominant pathogens: **Encapsulated bacteria**  
  - *Streptococcus pneumoniae*  
  - *Haemophilus influenzae*  
  - *Neisseria meningitidis*  

- Increased susceptibility to:  
  - Herpesviruses and other viruses  
  - *Pneumocystis jirovecii* (formerly *P. carinii*)

---

### <mark>Dermatitis</mark>
- Occurs in **~80% of patients**  
- Typically develops in the **first few months of life**  
- <mark>Often **severe and widespread**</mark>  
- Commonly affects:  
  - Face  
  - Scalp  
  - Flexural areas  

- Features distinguishing it from typical atopic dermatitis:  
  <mark>- More **exfoliative**</mark>  
  - **Serosanguineous crusting**  
  - Frequent **lichenification**  

- Complications:  
  - Secondary bacterial infection  
  - **Eczema herpeticum**  
  - **Molluscum contagiosum**  

- Additional IgE-mediated conditions:  
  - Urticaria  
  - Food allergies  
  - Asthma

---

### <mark>Autoimmune Manifestations</mark>
- Occur in **up to 40% of patients**  
- Most common:  
  - **Vasculitis** (20%) – affecting skin, GI tract, brain, heart  
  - **Autoimmune hemolytic anemia** (14%)  
  - **IgA nephropathy** (up to 10%)  

- Other immune-mediated conditions:  
  - Angioedema  
  - Dermatomyositis  
  - Pyoderma gangrenosum  
  - Erythema nodosum  

- Hepatosplenomegaly is common  
- Lymphadenopathy, transient arthritis, and joint effusions may occur

---

## <mark>Laboratory Findings</mark>

- **Thrombocytopenia** with **small platelets**  
- **Immunoglobulin abnormalities**:  
  - ↓ IgM (common)  
  - ↓ IgG (sometimes)  
  - Absent isohemagglutinins  
  - ↑ IgA, IgE, IgD  

- Impaired humoral and cellular immunity contributes to infection susceptibility and autoimmunity

--- 

*Note: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only curative therapy and is recommended early in the disease course.*

# Differential Diagnosis of Atopic Dermatitis

## Most Likely
- Contact dermatitis (allergic and irritant)  
- Seborrheic dermatitis  
- Scabies  
- Psoriasis  
- Ichthyosis vulgaris  
- Keratosis pilaris  
- Dermatophytosis  

## Consider
- Asteatotic eczema  
- Lichen simplex chronicus  
- Nummular dermatitis  
- Juvenile palmar-plantar dermatosis  
- Impetigo  
- Drug eruptions  
- Perioral dermatitis  
- Pityriasis alba  
- Photosensitivity disorders (hydroa vacciniforme, polymorphous light eruption, porphyrias)  
- Molluscum dermatitis  

## Less Common/Rare Disorders Predominantly in Adolescents and Adults
- Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides or Sézary syndrome)  
- Human immunodeficiency virus–associated dermatoses  
- Lupus erythematosus  
- Dermatomyositis  
- Graft-versus-host disease  
- Pemphigus foliaceus  
- Dermatitis herpetiformis  
- Photosensitivity disorders (hydroa vacciniforme, polymorphous light eruption, porphyrias)  

## Complications

### Ocular Problems
Eye complications associated with severe atopic dermatitis can lead to significant morbidity. Eyelid dermatitis and chronic blepharitis are commonly seen and may result in visual impairment due to corneal scarring. Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is typically bilateral and can cause disabling symptoms such as itching, burning, tearing, and copious mucoid discharge.

---

<mark>Infants presenting in the first year of life with failure to thrive, diarrhea, generalized scaling erythematous rash, and recurrent cutaneous or systemic infections should be evaluated for severe combined immunodeficiency syndrome.</mark> <mark>Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder, presents with cutaneous findings nearly indistinguishable from atopic dermatitis.</mark> <mark>It is associated with thrombocytopenia, variable abnormalities in humoral and cellular immunity, and recurrent severe bacterial infections.</mark>

<mark>Hyper-IgE syndrome is characterized by elevated serum IgE levels, defective T-cell function, and recurrent deep-seated bacterial infections, including cutaneous abscesses caused by *Staphylococcus aureus* or pruritic skin disease due to *S.</mark> <mark>aureus* pustulosis, or recalcitrant dermatophytosis.</mark> <mark>A papulopustular eruption on the face and scalp may appear in early life.</mark> <mark>Although *S.</mark> <mark>aureus* is a major pathogen, infections with other bacteria, viruses, and fungi may occur—especially in patients on long-term anti-staphylococcal antibiotic prophylaxis.</mark> <mark>Additional features include pneumonia with pneumatocele formation, dental anomalies with retained primary teeth, bone fractures, and osteopenia.</mark>

It is important to recognize that adults presenting with eczematous dermatitis without a history of childhood eczema, respiratory allergy, or atopic family history may have allergic contact dermatitis. A contact allergen should be suspected in any patient whose dermatitis fails to respond to appropriate therapy. Notably, contact allergy to topical glucocorticoids and topical calcineurin inhibitors has been reported in patients with chronic dermatitis. Additionally, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma must be ruled out in adults with chronic, treatment-resistant dermatitis. Skin biopsies should ideally be obtained from three separate sites, as histology may show spongiosis and inflammatory infiltrate resembling atopic dermatitis.

Eczematous dermatitis has also been reported in association with human immunodeficiency virus infection and various infestations, such as scabies. Other conditions that may mimic atopic dermatitis include psoriasis, ichthyoses, and seborrheic dermatitis.

# <mark>POSITION STATEMENT</mark>

## <mark>ETFAD/EADV Eczema Task Force 2020 Position Paper on Diagnosis and Treatment of Atopic Dermatitis in Adults and Children</mark>

### <mark>Abstract</mark>

**Atopic dermatitis (AD)** is a highly pruritic, chronic inflammatory skin disease. <mark>The diagnosis is made using established clinical criteria.</mark> <mark>Disease activity and burden are best assessed with a composite score that evaluates both objective and subjective symptoms, such as the **SCORing Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD)** index.</mark>

<mark>Management of AD must consider clinical and pathogenic variability, the patient’s age, and the goal of flare prevention.</mark> <mark>**Basic therapy** includes universal application of hydrating and barrier-stabilizing topical treatments, as well as avoidance of specific and non-specific triggering factors.</mark>

<mark>Visible skin lesions are treated with **anti-inflammatory topical agents**, including **corticosteroids** and **calcineurin inhibitors** (tacrolimus and pimecrolimus), the latter being preferred for sensitive areas such as the face and folds.</mark> <mark>**Topical tacrolimus** and certain mid-potency corticosteroids are evidence-based options for **proactive therapy**—defined as long-term, intermittent anti-inflammatory treatment of areas prone to frequent relapses.</mark>

**Systemic anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive treatments** are evolving rapidly and require careful monitoring. **Oral corticosteroids** have a largely unfavourable benefit-risk profile and should be avoided when possible. The **IL-4Rα blocker dupilumab** is a safe, effective, and licensed, though expensive, treatment option, with potential ocular side effects. Other emerging therapies include **biologics** targeting key pathways in the atopic immune response and various **Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors**.

**Dysbiosis** and skin infections can trigger disease exacerbations and may warrant adjunctive antimicrobial therapy. **Systemic antihistamines (H1-receptor blockers)** have limited efficacy in reducing AD-related itch and skin lesions.

**Adjuvant therapies** include **phototherapy**, preferably **narrowband UVB** or **UVA1**. **Coal tar** may be beneficial in atopic hand and foot eczema. **Dietary recommendations** should be individualized; elimination diets should only be implemented in cases of confirmed food allergy. **Allergen-specific immunotherapy** for aeroallergens may be considered in selected patients. **Psychosomatic counselling** is recommended to manage stress-induced flares.

Evidence-based **‘Eczema school’ educational programmes** and **therapeutic patient education** are strongly recommended for both children and adults.

---

### Introduction and Definitions

**Atopic dermatitis (AD)**, also known as atopic eczema, eczema, or neurodermitis, is an inflammatory, chronically relapsing, and intensely pruritic skin disorder that frequently occurs in families with a history of atopic diseases—such as AD, food allergy, bronchial asthma, or allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.

Current understanding positions AD as a **systemic Th2-driven disease**, with a high prevalence of atopic comorbidities, particularly in patients with moderate-to-severe disease. From a clinical and histopathological perspective, AD is characterized by **eosinophilic and spongiotic skin inflammation**, with distinct, age-dependent patterns in lesion distribution and morphology.

AD affects **2–10% of young adults** and up to **20% of children**, making it one of the most prevalent skin conditions worldwide. The diversity in proposed aetiological mechanisms is reflected in the various historical and regional terms used, including *neurodermitis* and *endogenous/constitutional eczema*.

**Atopy** is defined as a familial tendency toward hypersensitivity of the skin and mucosa to environmental antigens, typically associated with elevated **immunoglobulin E (IgE)** levels or altered pharmacological reactivity. The **ETFAD** defines atopy as the *"familial tendency to develop Th2 responses against common environmental antigens"*, encompassing both **IgE-mediated (extrinsic)** and **non-IgE-mediated (intrinsic)** subtypes of AD.

Atopic diseases are genetically linked, with a **concordance rate of 80% in monozygotic twins** compared to **30% in dizygotic twins**. Genetic polymorphisms associated with AD involve mediators of atopic inflammation across multiple chromosomes, some of which are also implicated in respiratory atopy.

# <mark>Guidelines for Treatment of Atopic Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis) – Part I</mark>

## <mark>Abstract</mark>

<mark>The evidence for the treatment of atopic eczema (atopic dermatitis, AE) is evaluated according to the Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation (AGREE) instrument.</mark> The consensus process included a nominal group technique and a DELPHI procedure. Management of AE must account for the individual variability in symptoms and disease course.

<mark>**Basic therapy** centers on regular use of hydrating topical agents and avoidance of specific and non-specific triggering factors.</mark> <mark>For flare-ups, **anti-inflammatory treatment** with topical glucocorticosteroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors (TCIs) is recommended.</mark> TCIs (tacrolimus and pimecrolimus) are increasingly used not only for exacerbations but also for proactive therapy in selected cases, particularly in sensitive areas such as the face and neck.

Topical corticosteroids remain the first-line anti-inflammatory treatment. However, TCIs are preferred in certain anatomical locations due to lower risk of skin atrophy. For severe, refractory cases, **systemic immunosuppressive therapy** may be considered.

Microbial colonization—especially by *Staphylococcus aureus*—and superinfection can trigger flares and may warrant adjunctive antimicrobial treatment. **Phototherapy**, particularly with UVA1 or narrowband UVB (311 nm), is an effective adjuvant option.

Dietary interventions should be implemented only in cases of confirmed food allergy. **Allergen-specific immunotherapy** to aeroallergens may benefit selected patients. Psychological stress can exacerbate AE, making **psychosomatic counseling** advisable in some cases. Structured patient education programs, such as **"eczema schools"**, have demonstrated efficacy.

Pruritus is a central symptom targeted by most therapies, but some patients require additional **antipruritic treatments**.

## Introduction

Atopic eczema (AE), also known as atopic dermatitis, eczema, or *Neurodermitis* in German-speaking countries, is a chronic or chronically relapsing, inflammatory, and intensely pruritic skin disorder. It frequently occurs in families with a history of other atopic conditions, such as bronchial asthma or allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.

AE is one of the most prevalent skin diseases worldwide, affecting up to **20% of children** and **1–3% of adults**. It often represents the initial stage of the "atopic march," preceding the development of allergic rhinitis and asthma.

Diagnosis of AE relies on established clinical criteria. There is no pathognomonic laboratory biomarker. While elevated total or allergen-specific IgE levels and positive skin prick tests are common, they are not universal. Patients without IgE sensitization are classified as having **intrinsic (non-IgE-associated) AE**, in contrast to the **extrinsic (IgE-associated) form**. This distinction remains debated but has practical implications for management, particularly regarding allergen avoidance strategies.

### Aetiopathophysiology

The development of AE involves a complex interplay of genetic, immunological, and environmental factors:

- **Genetic predisposition**: High heritability is evident, with 80% concordance in monozygotic twins versus 20% in dizygotic twins.  
- **Immune dysregulation**: Early disease stages are characterized by a Th2-dominant immune response, leading to increased IgE production.  
- **Skin barrier dysfunction**: Impaired barrier function results from abnormalities in lipid composition and structural proteins, including filaggrin mutations and deficiency in protease inhibitors, contributing to dry skin and increased allergen penetration.  
- **Microbial dysbiosis**: Abnormal colonization with pathogens such as *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Malassezia furfur*, instead of commensals like *Staphylococcus epidermidis*, increases infection risk and inflammation.  
- **Psychosomatic factors**: Stress influences disease activity via autonomic nervous system imbalance and increased release of inflammatory mediators from cells such as eosinophils.

Effective management of AE requires an individualized approach that addresses the specific pathogenic mechanisms present in each patient.

### Disease Severity Assessment

After diagnosis, assessment of disease severity is essential. The **Scoring Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD)** index, developed by the European Task Force on Atopic Dermatitis (ETFAD), is the standard tool for evaluating extent, intensity, and subjective symptoms (pruritus and sleep disturbance).

## Definition and Pathogenesis of Atopy

<mark>Atopy can be defined as a familial hypersensitivity of the skin and mucosa to environmental substances, associated with increased production of immunoglobulin E (IgE) or altered pharmacologic reactivity.</mark> <mark>The ETFAD defines atopy as the "familial tendency to develop Th2 responses against common environmental antigens," encompassing both IgE-associated (extrinsic) and non-IgE-associated (intrinsic) subtypes within the atopic spectrum.</mark>

## Genetic and Molecular Basis

Atopic diseases are genetically linked, with a concordance rate of 80% in monozygotic twins compared to 30% in dizygotic twins. Genetic polymorphisms involved in atopic dermatitis (AD) affect mediators of atopic inflammation located on various chromosomes, some of which are also implicated in respiratory atopy. The strongest genetic association is with mutations in the *filaggrin* gene, which is also linked to ichthyosis vulgaris, underscoring the role of epidermal barrier dysfunction in AD. Clinically, concomitant ichthyosis vulgaris may be identified by increased palmar hyperlinearity, a useful indicator of filaggrin gene mutations.

## <mark>Clinical Presentation</mark>

<mark>In early infancy, AD may present as "cradle cap"—a yellowish, seborrheic, crusted scaling on the scalp—which typically responds to emollient therapy alone.</mark> <mark>The disease usually begins on the face (with relative sparing of the middle face), extensor surfaces of the limbs, and trunk, often with oozing and crusting.</mark> <mark>As the child grows, involvement shifts to the flexural areas, neck, and hands, accompanied by dry skin.</mark>

<mark>Skin barrier dysfunction in AD is evidenced by increased transepidermal water loss (TEWL).</mark> <mark>Measuring TEWL with an evaporimeter and discussing results with patients can enhance adherence to emollient therapy.</mark> <mark>Lichenification results from chronic scratching and rubbing, often occurring at night.</mark> <mark>The prurigo variant of AD is characterized by excoriated, nodular, and lichenified lesions.</mark>

<mark>Exacerbations typically begin with intense pruritus in the absence of visible lesions, followed by erythema, papules, and infiltration.</mark> Histopathologic findings are not specific for AD; thus, routine biopsy is not diagnostic but may help exclude conditions such as cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in adults.

## <mark>Diagnosis</mark>

<mark>In the absence of a specific laboratory marker, AD is diagnosed clinically.</mark> <mark>While an experienced clinician’s judgment surpasses available diagnostic criteria, standardized criteria are essential for epidemiological studies and clinical trial enrollment.</mark> <mark>Most criteria focus on cutaneous signs of atopy.</mark>

- <mark>**Hanifin and Rajka criteria** require three of the following four: pruritus, typical morphology and distribution, chronic or relapsing course, and personal or family history of atopy. Additionally, at least three minor criteria from a list of 21 must be fulfilled.</mark>
- <mark>**UK Working Party criteria** include an itchy skin condition in the past 12 months plus at least three of the following: onset before age two, history of skin fold involvement, generalized dry skin, personal or family history of other atopic diseases, and visible flexural eczema.</mark>

## <mark>Impact on Quality of Life</mark>

Atopic dermatitis significantly affects all aspects of a patient’s life. Moderate-to-severe AD is associated with depression, anxiety, reduced quality of life, impaired self-esteem, and increased suicide risk. The social burden of moderate-to-severe AD is comparable to that of psoriasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes.

## Management of Flares

Managing acute exacerbations (flares) of AD is challenging, requiring rapid symptom control without disrupting long-term management goals such as flare prevention and minimizing treatment side effects. Flares may reveal underlying triggers, including allergies or infections. Therefore, initial evaluation should include a detailed history of flare circumstances and a thorough dermatologic examination, including assessment of lymph nodes, orifices, and skin folds. A professional and empathetic approach during flare management lays the foundation for future treatment adherence.

## Staphylococcal Bacteremia in HIV Disease

Staphylococcal bacteremia may complicate either primary or secondary cutaneous infections such as psoriasis or scabies. However, the most common source of hematogenous dissemination is an intravenous catheter, accounting for 73 percent of bacteremia cases. <mark>As with most infections in HIV disease, staphylococcal infections are frequently recurrent.</mark>

Management (see Chap. 177) should include:
- Treatment of the acute infection
- Management of underlying dermatoses
- Eradication of nasal *S. aureus* carriage using mupirocin (pseudomonic acid) ointment
- Long-term oral prophylaxis for recurrent infections

---

## *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* Infections in HIV Disease

*Pseudomonas aeruginosa* (see Chap. 180) can cause primary cutaneous infections such as cellulitis (e.g., ecthyma gangrenosum), catheter-site infections, and secondary infections of underlying skin conditions like Kaposi sarcoma in advanced HIV disease.

Cutaneous *P. aeruginosa* infection occurs via:
- Local invasion through skin breaches
- Primary infection of skin appendages in the anogenital or axillary regions
- Hematogenous dissemination to the skin

These infections may progress to bacteremia, leading to seeding of multiple organ systems.

---

## Tuberculosis and Other Mycobacterial Infections in HIV Disease

Tuberculosis is the most common opportunistic infection in HIV-infected individuals in developing countries. While cutaneous tuberculosis (see Chap. 184) is relatively uncommon, the incidence of extrapulmonary tuberculosis is higher in HIV-positive individuals:
- 15% in non-HIV-infected individuals
- 20% to 40% in those with HIV disease
- Up to 70% in advanced HIV disease

Non-tuberculous (environmental) mycobacteria reported to cause cutaneous lesions in HIV disease include:
- *M. chelonae*
- *M. fortuitum*
- *M. kansasii*
- *M. malmoense*
- *M. gordonae*
- *M. marinum*
- *M. haemophilum*

The most common non-tuberculous mycobacterial pathogen in advanced HIV disease is the *M. avium-intracellulare* complex (MAC). However, MAC rarely presents with cutaneous manifestations. The incidence of MAC infection has declined due to primary prophylaxis with azithromycin and, more recently, effective antiretroviral therapy (HAART).

---

## <mark>Bacillary Angiomatosis and Bacillary Peliosis in HIV Disease</mark>

<mark>Bacillary angiomatosis (BA) and bacillary peliosis (see Chap.</mark> <mark>182), caused by *Bartonella henselae* and *B.</mark> <mark>quintana*, occur predominantly in the setting of advanced HIV-induced immunodeficiency.</mark>

### <mark>Clinical Features of Bacillary Angiomatosis</mark>

- <mark>Angioproliferative skin lesions resembling:</mark>
  <mark>- Cherry hemangiomas</mark>
  <mark>- Pyogenic granulomas</mark>
  <mark>- Kaposi sarcoma</mark>
- <mark>Cutaneous lesions are red to violaceous, dome-shaped papules, nodules, or plaques</mark>
- <mark>Lesion size ranges from a few millimeters to 2–3 cm in diameter</mark>
- <mark>Dermal vascular lesions with thinned or eroded epidermis</mark>
- <mark>Subcutaneous nodular lesions may also occur, sometimes lacking the typical red appearance</mark>
- <mark>Lesions are soft to firm and may be tender</mark>
- <mark>Number of lesions varies from solitary to over 100; in rare cases, more than 1000</mark>

<mark>Currently, the prevalence of BA in North America and Western Europe is very low, largely due to improved immune function from HAART and prophylactic strategies targeting opportunistic infections.</mark>

# Dermoscopy and In Vivo Imaging

Dermoscopy is more sensitive than visual inspection in detecting orifices, vessels, and specific vascular patterns such as crown, radial, flower, and punctiform arrangements.

In vivo confocal microscopy reveals a round, well-circumscribed lesion with central cystic areas filled with brightly refractile material, corresponding to molluscum bodies seen on histopathology.

# Laboratory

Laboratory testing is not routinely required for the diagnosis of molluscum contagiosum, as clinical and dermoscopic evaluation is typically sufficient.

In uncertain cases, confirmation can be achieved through histological examination, polymerase chain reaction, or electron microscopy. Histology shows the characteristic "nuts in a sack" pattern. Electron microscopy identifies the brick-shaped virions of molluscum contagiosum virus.

# Histopathology

Haematoxylin and eosin staining of molluscum contagiosum lesions typically shows a crateriform, hyperplastic epidermis or endophytic infundibular hyperplasia, forming a circumscribed cup-shaped pseudotumor. This structure contains large cells with granular, eosinophilic intracytoplasmic molluscum bodies (also known as inclusion bodies or Henderson-Paterson bodies). These inclusion bodies can measure up to 35 microns in diameter and consist of millions of virions that compress the keratinocyte nuclei. They progressively enlarge and become basophilic before being released onto the skin surface.

Unusual histological variants include pseudocystic, giant, and pedunculated forms. Disseminated, confluent, or atypical giant lesions may indicate immunosuppression, particularly HIV infection.

Special stains such as Lendrum's phloxine tartrazine or toluidine blue/Giemsa are rarely needed, as inclusion bodies are usually evident on routine staining. However, these stains may be helpful when folliculitis, abscess formation following follicular rupture, or a dense inflammatory infiltrate obscure the inclusions.

Occasionally, a dense dermal lymphocytic infiltrate with CD30-positive cells may mimic anaplastic large cell lymphoma or lymphomatoid papulosis. Molluscum bodies can be identified by immunohistochemistry on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue, and cross-reactivity with Melan A—a melanocytic marker—has been reported.

Immunohistochemical studies are reserved for research and not used in routine diagnosis. Additional histological findings may include perilesional fibro-oedematous to fibromyxoid stroma, and rarely amyloid-like deposits, anetoderma, or metaplastic ossification. Follicular induction in the adjacent epidermis should not be mistaken for basal cell carcinoma.

In approximately 4% of cases, molluscum contagiosum may coexist with other lesions such as epidermal cysts or melanocytic naevi, potentially masking the characteristic changes. Coinfection with other pathogens—such as human papillomavirus or *Cryptococcus neoformans*—within the same lesion can occur, especially in immunocompromised individuals.

# Differential Diagnosis

Molluscum contagiosum must be differentiated from other conditions, particularly in the setting of possible sexual transmission.

In immunocompetent patients, mimickers include:
- Genital warts (condyloma acuminata)
- Flat warts
- Lichen planus
- Lichen nitidus
- Condylomata lata of secondary syphilis
- Pyogenic granuloma
- Ectopic sebaceous glands
- Dermal cyst
- Vulvar lymphangioma circumscriptum
- Keratoacanthoma
- Basal cell carcinoma
- Amelanotic melanoma

In immunosuppressed patients, opportunistic infections that may resemble molluscum contagiosum include:
- *Penicillium marneffei* (penicilliosis)
- *Cryptococcus neoformans* (cryptococcosis)
- *Coccidioides* spp. (coccidioidomycosis)
- *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis*
- *Aspergillus fumigatus* (aspergillosis)
- *Sporothrix schenckii*
